extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; readers interested in ancient Greek and Egyptian mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Pythagorean arithmetic and the earliest Greek geometry (Nicomachus, Theon, Iamblichus, Egyptian mensuration). Contains definitions, formulae, propositions, and historical commentary about ancient methods of number representation and area measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gnomons for polygonal numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: The gnomons (incremental figures) that generate polygonal numbers are: for triangles the successive natural numbers 1,2,3,...; for squares the successive odd numbers 1,3,5,...; for pentagonal numbers the arithmetic progression 1,4,7, ...; and generally for a-gonal numbers the sequence 1, 1+(a-2), 1+2(a-2), ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how polygonal numbers are formed by adding successive gnomons; used as the basis for geometrical/arithmetic representations of polygonal sequences. Nicomachus lists examples up to heptagons.

rubrics_metrics.name: General formula for an a-gonal number of side n
rubrics_metrics.description: The a-gonal (a-sided polygonal) number with side n equals n + n(n-1)(a-2)/2 (i.e. n + ½ n(n-1)(a-2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nicomachus states the summation that yields this expression (though he does not give the general formula explicitly in his text); the formula follows from summing the gnomons 1 + [1+(a-2)] + ... + [1+(n-1)(a-2)].

rubrics_metrics.name: Squares as sum of two consecutive triangular numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Any square n^2 can be expressed as the sum of two successive triangular numbers: n^2 = T_{n-1} + T_n, where T_k = k(k+1)/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nicomachus mentions explicitly n^2 = ½(n-1)n + ½n(n+1); Iamblichus illustrates this as a 'race-course' construction (up to n and back down) giving a geometric intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pyramidal (solid) numbers from polygonal bases
rubrics_metrics.description: A pyramid (solid number) with a polygonal base of side n is obtained by stacking similar polygons with sides n, n-1, ..., down to 1; the pyramid equals the sum of the polygonal numbers of those sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text describes the construction (triangular/ square/other polygonal bases) and names truncated variants (once-truncated, twice-truncated, etc.). Nicomachus gives examples for triangular pyramids but not a compact general summation formula; a summation expression is indicated in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of solid numbers (cubes, scalene, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cubes are products of three equal factors; scalene numbers are products of three unequal factors and have been termed wedges, stakes, or altars (though some of these names imply tapering solids rather than mere products). Other varieties include parallelepipeds, beams/columns of form m(m+ n), tiles of form m(m-n), recurring cubes whose last digits are 1,5,6, and 'circular' squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion connects algebraic factor forms with geometric/figurative names used in ancient sources and clarifies terminological misapprehensions (e.g., geometrical tapering implied by some names). Examples of forms and digit-ending properties are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations among oblong, square, and triangular numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Oblong (pronic) numbers are n(n+1); triangular numbers T_n = n(n+1)/2. Various simple formulae relate these sequences (examples given in the text include algebraic identities connecting successive terms and ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific algebraic equalities are listed in the source (some notation in the edition is compressed), and these relations are 'easily verified' by elementary algebra; the text uses these to motivate geometric demonstrations with gnomons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cubes as sums of consecutive odd numbers (construction and consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each cube n^3 can be represented as the sum of n consecutive odd numbers (e.g., 2^3 = 3+5, 3^3 = 7+9+11, 4^3 = 13+15+17+19). Consequently the sum of cubes 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + r^3 equals the square of the triangular sum: (1+2+...+r)^2 = [r(r+1)/2]^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nicomachus states the empirical pattern; the text gives a proof by grouping odd numbers into gnomons around a central square and shows how counting terms leads to the usual formula for the sum of cubes. Historical note: Romans and later medieval writers knew the summation even if Nicomachus did not explicitly state the final algebraic formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic- and geometric-progression identities and mean properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If three numbers a,b,c are in arithmetical progression (a-b = b-c), geometrical progression (common ratio r), or harmonic progression, certain algebraic identities follow (e.g., for geometric progression with ratio r, (a-b) = (r-1)b and (b-c) = (r-1)c and related expressions for b in terms of a,c and r).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nicomachus records these relations and notes correspondences between the three types of progression, including inequalities depending on order and the Platonic theorem concerning possible geometric means between square and cube numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue forms of square numbers (Theon of Smyrna / Lamblichus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Square numbers cannot be congruent to 3n+2, 4n+2, or 4n+3. For any integer m either m^2 or m^2 - 1 is divisible by 3, and likewise either m^2 or m^2 - 1 is divisible by 4. Theon divides squares into four canonical residue-forms with associated integrality properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows how writing integers in residue classes (mod 3 and mod 4, or mod 6) yields the four possible algebraic forms for squares and proves the non-existence of certain residues for squares; references to Theon and Iamblichus are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iamblichus' 'race-course' representation of a square
rubrics_metrics.description: Iamblichus presents n^2 as the sum of a rising sequence 1+2+...+n and a descending sequence 1+2+...+(n-1) (visualized as out-and-back), giving a geometric picture for n^2 = T_n + T_{n-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as pedagogical/geometric intuition for square decomposition and to relate to Pythagorean decimal terminology and units of courses (10,100,1000 as units of successive 'courses').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean digit-sum (pythmen) and casting-out-nines property
rubrics_metrics.description: The iterative sum of the decimal digits of a number (pythmen) yields a number congruent mod 9 to the original number; repeated digit-sums reduce a number to its residue modulo 9. In particular, the sum of three consecutive integers whose largest is divisible by 3 reduces (by iterated digit-sum) to 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamblichus' explanation uses congruences mod 9 to formalize the procedure. The text connects this Pythagorean method to later practices ('casting out nines') and to the 'pythmen' method used for names in certain divination/calculation texts (Hippolytus excerpt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean calculus for names (alphabetical numeration and digit reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign letter-values, sum them to obtain a number, then reduce by iterated digit-sum or division by 9 (or 7 for the 'rule of seven') to obtain the 'pythmen' (a single-digit characteristic). If the sum divides exactly by 9, the pythmen is taken as 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: name sums 36 -> digits 3+6 = 9; sum 19 -> 1+9 = 10 -> 1+0 =1; alternative practical rule: take remainder mod 9 (zero interpreted as 9). Hippolytus records this as used in Pythagorean/occult computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egyptian rectangle and triangle area rules (Papyrus Rhind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rectangle area is product of side-numbers. Triangle area is given as 1/2 * base * 'side' (interpreted by some scholars as half-base times height); trapezium area is given as 1/2*(a+c)*h (where a,c are parallel sides and h is the 'side' marked), though interpretations differ about whether the diagrams are right or isosceles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars debate whether the Rhind formulas assume right angles (making them exact) or are crude approximations for general isosceles figures; comparisons with Edfu inscriptions show some persistent approximate rules in Egyptian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egyptian approximate quadrilateral area formula (Edfu inscriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A frequently used formula in Edfu inscriptions for the area of a quadrilateral with successive sides a,b,c,d is given as ((a + c)/2) * ((b + d)/2) (often written in text as (a + c) . (b + d) in their notation), an approximation treating the figure like an averaged rectangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from inscriptions are cited showing the formula used for many plots even when the true shape is not a perfect trapezium; later Edfu texts sometimes avoid the approximation or apply root approximations for more accurate measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egyptian circle area approximation (Rhind papyrus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rhind papyrus gives a rule for the area of a circle as [ (8/9) * diameter ]^2, which corresponds to taking π ≈ 3.1605... (often cited as 3.16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This value is inferred from the papyrus' instruction to take 8/9 of the diameter and square it; the text notes alternative inferences from other measurements but emphasizes the close numerical approximation to π derived from the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rope-stretching and knowledge of a 3-4-5 right triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Egyptian 'rope-stretchers' (harpedonaptae) used ropes and pegs to layout angles; evidence suggests they knew the 3,4,5 integer right triangle relation (a^2 + b^2 = c^2) and could construct right angles practically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and pictorial evidence (inscriptions, rope-stretching scenes, Berlin leather inscription) support practical surveying techniques; comparison with Indian and Chinese practices suggests cross-cultural practical methods for right-angle construction.
